title: Three perfect days in Paris
dek: A long Toussaint weekend of Zurbarán, Cassatt and Cézanne, walk-in bistro lunches, chocolate at Porte de Versailles and chrysanthemums in Montmartre.

hero.caption: Pont Alexandre III, with the Grand Palais beyond, where “Cézanne et nous” runs until January.

intro:
This is a three-day weekend in France. Sunday, November 1, is **Toussaint**, All Saints' Day, a public holiday, and it closes out the autumn school break that began on October 17. Parisian families will be squeezing in one last museum before classes resume on Monday, so book anything with a timed ticket now. The clocks went back last Sunday, which means the light is gone by about a quarter past five: plan the walking for the middle of the day and keep the late afternoon for galleries.

And the galleries are the reason to come. The autumn shows have all just opened and none is about to close. The Louvre has *Zurbarán 1598–1664* under the pyramid, the Musée d'Orsay has some 80 works by Mary Cassatt, and the restored Grand Palais has *Cézanne et nous*, nearly 180 pieces tracing what painters from Matisse to Peter Doig took from him. Across town the Salon du Chocolat fills Paris Expo Porte de Versailles until Sunday, and Halloween on Saturday is a modest affair here, more costume parties than trick-or-treating.

Paris has had a rough fortnight. Rioting and looting on October 17 and 18 led the Police Prefecture to impose a night curfew on the central island of Place de la République and the southern edge of Les Halles. The latest order ran to October 26 and the prefecture says it will stay "as long as necessary", so this plan keeps its evenings on the Left Bank, around the Louvre and up in Montmartre. Friday is Saint-Germain, Saturday the Louvre and the Right Bank, and Sunday belongs to Montmartre, where the cemetery fills with flowers for the holiday.

days.title: Friday: Saint-Germain and the Left Bank
days.intro: Impressionists in the morning, a walk-in bistro lunch, the Luxembourg garden while the light lasts, and a long dinner near the Invalides.

stops.name: Café de Flore
stops.text: Yes, it is the famous one, and it earns a single breakfast for the room itself: red banquettes, mirrors, waiters in long aprons, and a terrace that has watched the boulevard since the 1880s. Order coffee and soft-boiled eggs (about €13.50 for two) or a buttered ham baguette and take a window seat. It is not cheap and the food is plain brasserie cooking. Opens at 7:30 daily; at nine on a Friday you should get a table without waiting.

stops.name: Musée d'Orsay
stops.text: Go straight to **Mary Cassatt: Being Independent** (until January 31), about 80 paintings, pastels and prints from the American who joined the Impressionists in Paris, including her *Young Girl with a Banjo*, which the museum acquired this year. The show also covers *Modern Woman*, her lost mural for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair. Then climb to the fifth floor for the permanent Impressionist rooms and the view through the great clock. Open 9:30 to 18:00 Friday; closed Mondays, so not an option on November 2.

stops.name: Le Comptoir du Relais
stops.text: The bistro that Yves Camdeborde made famous is still the Left Bank's best argument for lunch without a booking: it takes no reservations, so you queue on the pavement and are rewarded with a short, market-driven menu of chalked specials and natural wines in a tiny room. Order whatever the day's market has brought, and expect neighbours elbow to elbow. Lunch runs from noon into the afternoon; arriving just after the 13:00 rush usually shortens the wait.

stops.name: Jardin du Luxembourg
stops.addr: Rue de Médicis / Rue de Vaugirard
stops.text: Ten minutes up Rue de Condé brings you to the Senate's garden at its autumn best: chestnuts turning, the green metal chairs pulled into the last sun around the octagonal basin, chess players under the trees near the tennis courts, and the Medici Fountain in shadow. Entry is free. Gates close at dusk, which now comes early, so treat this as a ninety-minute stroll and watch for the warden's whistle. The garden was shut on October 24 for demonstrations; check the Senate site the morning you go.

stops.name: Le Bon Marché Rive Gauche
stops.text: Paris's oldest department store, founded in 1852, is a good place to warm up as the light goes. Since October 24 it has been dressed as a snowy mountain village for Christmas, with the animated windows due in November. Next door, the food hall La Grande Épicerie is the place for edible souvenirs to carry home. Open until 20:00 Friday and Saturday, and 11:00 to 20:00 on Sundays.

stops.name: Le Violon d'Ingres
stops.text: Christian Constant's restaurant in the shadow of the Eiffel Tower is a grown-up dining room with a menu that doesn't chase trends. The house classics are the ones to order, among them pan-seared duck foie gras and crisp-skinned sea bass. It is open every day for dinner from 18:30 to 22:00, which makes it a useful booking on a holiday weekend. Reserve online; walk to the tower's light show afterwards.

stops.name: Prescription Cocktail Club
stops.text: A short taxi ride brings you back to Saint-Germain for a nightcap at the Experimental group's Left Bank bar: draped fabric, upholstered walls, small sofas tucked into corners and a menu by Maxime Potfer that mixes house signatures with reworked classics. If you're still hungry, there is a cheddar croque. It is open until 4:00 on Fridays, and it fills from about ten, so come straight after dinner.

days.title: Saturday: the Louvre and the Right Bank
days.intro: The first slot at the Louvre, a croque at Paris's oldest coffee roaster, covered passages, Cézanne, and a long Halloween dinner across from the museum.

stops.name: Louvre
stops.text: From October 17 to November 1 the Louvre requires a booked time slot for every visitor, free entries included, so book the 9:00 opening now at ticket.louvre.fr and nowhere else (the museum warns against resellers and mirror sites). Start in the Hall Napoléon with **Zurbarán 1598–1664**, the Spanish painter's retrospective, co-organised with London's National Gallery and the Art Institute of Chicago, before the galleries upstairs fill. Adult tickets are €22 for EEA residents and €32 for other visitors. Open until 18:00 Saturday; closed Tuesdays.

stops.name: Café Verlet
stops.text: Five minutes up Rue de Rivoli, this coffee house has been roasting beans on Rue Saint-Honoré since 1880, and still does it on site. Lunch is simple: a croque-monsieur (€18) or croque-madame, then a slice of the Moka Verlet, a sponge layered with Sidamo coffee cream. Buy a bag of beans on the way out. Open Monday to Saturday, 10:00 to 19:00, and closed Sunday, so today is the day for it.

stops.name: Palais-Royal and Galerie Vivienne
stops.addr: Place du Palais-Royal / 4 Rue des Petits-Champs
stops.text: Walk through the Palais-Royal: Daniel Buren's striped columns in the main courtyard, then the long garden of clipped limes inside its arcades, where the shops sell gloves, vintage dresses and tin soldiers. Leave by the north end and cross Rue des Petits-Champs to the Galerie Vivienne, an 1820s covered passage with a mosaic floor and a glass roof, home to bookshops and a wine merchant. It is all free, and covered if it rains.

stops.name: Grand Palais: Cézanne et nous
stops.text: Line 1 from Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre takes you to Champs-Élysées–Clemenceau in minutes. *Cézanne et nous* gathers nearly 180 works to show what painters took from him, from Gauguin, Matisse, Picasso and Mondrian to Joan Mitchell, Bridget Riley and Peter Doig. It is co-produced with the Centre Pompidou, whose own building is closed for renovation until 2030, and the Musée d'Orsay. Allow ninety minutes. Entry is from Avenue du Général Eisenhower; open 10:00 to 19:30 Saturday, until 22:00 on Fridays.

stops.name: Le Fumoir
stops.text: Facing the Louvre's east colonnade, Le Fumoir has a long bar in front, a library room behind and a Swedish streak in the kitchen. Start with marinated herring and creamed cucumber, then sea bass with crisp skin and spiced lentils, and finish with the kladdkaka, a sticky Swedish chocolate cake. On Halloween night it is a grown-up refuge from the costume parties. Book the dining room online; the bar takes walk-ins only.

stops.name: Cour Carrée and Pont des Arts
stops.text: Step out of Le Fumoir and into the Louvre's Cour Carrée, the square Renaissance courtyard, which is usually quiet and softly lit at this hour. Walk through to the Seine and onto the Pont des Arts, the iron footbridge to the Institut de France, for the view upstream to the Île de la Cité and the restored spire of Notre-Dame. From the Left Bank end, Saint-Germain's cafés are five minutes away if the night isn't over.

days.title: Sunday: Montmartre for Toussaint
days.intro: All Saints' Day on the hill: crêpes, the basilica, a museum in Renoir's old studio, a cheap lunch at the bottom of the hill, and the cemetery in its flowers.

stops.name: Breizh Café Abbesses
stops.text: Bertrand Larcher's Breton crêperie opens at 9:00 every day, which makes it a dependable holiday breakfast near the foot of the hill. Order a buckwheat galette with egg and Comté, or a plain butter-sugar crêpe made with good salted butter, and a bowl of farmhouse cider if you are being Breton about it. It sits at the corner of Rue Yvonne Le Tac, a short walk from the Wall of Love in Square Jehan Rictus. Book ahead; the room is small.

stops.name: Sacré-Cœur and Place du Tertre
stops.text: Climb the steps (or take the funicular on a metro ticket) to the white basilica and the long view south over the city, best before the crowds peak at midday. Then wander west past the painters' easels on Place du Tertre, down Rue de l'Abreuvoir and around the Montmartre vineyard. Toussaint is a holy day and the basilica will be holding Masses, so keep voices down and photos discreet inside.

stops.name: Musée de Montmartre
stops.text: A 17th-century house where Renoir painted and Suzanne Valadon and her son Maurice Utrillo later lived and worked, now tells the story of Montmartre's cabarets and artists, with Valadon's restored studio upstairs and gardens looking out over the vineyard. It is open every day, 10:00 to 19:00, with last entry 45 minutes before closing; full price is €16. The garden café, Café Renoir, serves Wednesday to Sunday from 11:00 to 17:00.

stops.name: Bouillon Pigalle
stops.text: Walk down Rue Lepic to the boulevard for the city's best-value lunch: a modern take on the old workers' bouillon, with paper tablecloths and brisk waiters. Gault&Millau lists bœuf bourguignon with coquillettes at €12.20, terrine with green peppercorns at €5.40 and île flottante at €3.20, so a full meal comes to about €20. It opens at 11:30 on weekends and holidays and runs all day; the queue moves, but booking online removes it.

stops.name: Montmartre Cemetery
stops.text: Toussaint is when France visits its dead, and the city expects more than 200,000 people in its cemeteries this weekend, carrying pots of chrysanthemums. Montmartre's sunken cemetery, under the iron bridge of Rue Caulaincourt, holds Degas, Stendhal, Berlioz, François Truffaut and Dalida. Walk quietly and give families space at the graves. The gates are open 9:00 to 18:00 on November 1 (8:30 to 18:00 on Saturday), staff at the entrance on Avenue Rachel can help you find a grave, and cars are banned inside.

stops.name: La Mascotte
stops.text: Plenty of Paris shuts on a holiday Sunday night. La Mascotte doesn't: this old Montmartre brasserie is open 7:00 to midnight every day. Sit in the middle room, which suits a moderate budget, and order Breton oysters, Normandy mussels with cream and fries, or Loctudy sole carved at the trolley, with a reasonably priced Beaujolais cru. Finish with Berthillon ice cream. Book by phone on 01 46 06 28 15; Abbesses metro is a few doors away.

stay.name: Mandarin Oriental Lutetia, Paris
stay.text: The Left Bank's grand hotel, open since 1910 and restored by Jean-Michel Wilmotte, now trades under the Mandarin Oriental name. It puts you a short walk from Friday's whole day and facing Le Bon Marché across Square Boucicaut. There is a 17-metre pool for a grey November morning, Bar Joséphine for jazz and cocktails, and a weekend tea in the library salon.

stay.name: Le Relais Saint-Germain
stay.text: Twenty-two rooms in a late-16th-century building on the Carrefour de l'Odéon, each one different, with old beams and panelling, and named after a writer. Above all, it belongs to the same house as Le Comptoir du Relais downstairs, and guests can order the bistro's food to their room. Note that the hotel is not accessible for guests with reduced mobility.

stay.name: Hôtel Rochechouart
stay.text: A 1920s Art Deco hotel on Boulevard de Rochechouart, at the foot of Montmartre and a Design Hotels member, which puts Sunday on your doorstep and line 2 of the metro outside. Rooms are small, as an April 2026 review noted; the bistro downstairs and the old Mikado ballroom make up for it. The rooftop with its Sacré-Cœur view usually opens only in warmer months.

events.name: Salon du Chocolat et de la Pâtisserie
events.text: The 31st edition of the chocolate and pastry fair: chocolatiers, pâtissiers, demonstrations and tastings. Weekend adult tickets are €20 (weekdays €16), and a cheaper late-day ticket covers 5 to 7 p.m. Metro line 12 or tram T2/T3a to Porte de Versailles.

events.name: ARTE Concert Festival
events.text: Two free nights from the Franco-German broadcaster: Kneecap, Only Real and Tramhaus on Friday; Uche Yara, Uzi Freyja and Shygirl on Saturday, plus talks and a masterclass with Nicolas Godin. Entry is free but must be reserved, and places are limited.

events.name: Rolex Paris Masters: qualifying
events.text: The last ATP Masters 1000 of the season begins with two days of singles qualifying, a cheaper way to see top players up close; the main draw starts Monday, November 2, and the final is on November 8.

events.name: Paris Ekiden
events.text: A marathon relay run by teams of six, past the Eiffel Tower, the Trocadéro and the Invalides. Expect closed riverside roads on the Left Bank on Sunday morning, and allow extra time for taxis.

events.name: Toussaint in the cemeteries
events.text: The city expects more than 200,000 visitors to its cemeteries around All Saints' Day. The main cemeteries are open 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday, with free shuttles inside the largest.

events.name: Last day: Video Games & Music
events.text: The Philharmonie's exhibition on music in video games, open since April, ends this weekend. It's a good holiday outing with teenagers at La Villette; book a slot.

know: **From CDG:** RER B runs to Gare du Nord, Châtelet and Saint-Michel–Notre-Dame; the airport ticket is €14 in 2026. On weekday evenings until November 10 the line is cut between Châtelet–Les Halles and the airport from 22:45, with replacement buses, so a late Friday arrival means a bus or a taxi. Official taxi flat fares are €56 to the Right Bank and €65 to the Left Bank, day or night.

**From Orly:** Metro line 14 now runs from Orly into central Paris (Châtelet, Pyramides, Saint-Lazare) on the same €14 airport ticket, and the Orlyval shuttle still links to RER B at Antony. Taxi flat fares from Orly are €36 to the Left Bank and €45 to the Right Bank.

**Tickets:** A single metro-RER ticket costs €2.55 in 2026 and paper tickets have been phased out; load tickets onto a Navigo Easy card from any station machine. Two station closures affect this plan's neighbourhoods: Saint-Michel on line 4 (until December 19) and République on line 8. Line 13 skips Porte de Clichy through Sunday.

**Toussaint:** Sunday, November 1, is a public holiday and the last day of the school break. The Louvre, Orsay, Grand Palais, Musée de Montmartre and Bon Marché are all open, but many independent restaurants and shops close on Sundays anyway; book Sunday meals. On Monday the Musée d'Orsay is closed, as on every Monday.

**The curfew:** After rioting on October 17 and 18 the Police Prefecture imposed an 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew on the central island of Place de la République and the southern part of Les Halles, plus bans on undeclared demonstrations, renewed "as long as necessary". The last published order ran to October 26. Check the prefecture's news before going out late, and expect some central stations to close early on short notice, as Châtelet and République did from October 23 to 25.

**Strikes:** No transport strike is called for this weekend. French rail unions have called a national SNCF strike for Thursday, November 5, which may affect TGV, RER and Transilien trains, so check if you're leaving by train or staying on.
**Tipping:** Service is included by law in French bills. Rounding up or leaving a euro or two for coffee, or a few euros after a good dinner, is a courtesy, never an obligation.
**Daylight:** France moved its clocks back an hour on October 25. It is dark by about 17:15, so do the parks and the hill walks before mid-afternoon.
